event: The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps conducted military strikes against a Kurdish opposition group headquarters located in the Sulaymaniyah Governorate of Iraq's Kurdistan region.

verified_facts.statement: The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) conducted military strikes using missiles and/or drones against targets in the Sulaymaniyah Governorate of Iraq's Kurdistan Region.
verified_facts.note: Confirmed by international news agencies, Iraqi government statements, and IRGC announcements. Specific dates and casualty figures vary by source.

verified_facts.statement: The strikes targeted locations associated with Kurdish opposition groups, including facilities in or near Sulaymaniyah.
verified_facts.note: Confirmed by multiple sources; the specific groups named (PJAK, KDP-I, others) are consistently identified as targets.

verified_facts.statement: Civilian areas, including residential neighborhoods and refugee camps, were present in or near the strike zones.
verified_facts.source_url: https://www.hrw.org or https://www.amnesty.org reports; UNHCR statements
verified_facts.note: Documented by human rights organizations and UN agencies; the degree of intentional targeting vs. proximity remains disputed.

verified_facts.statement: Multiple strikes occurred both before and after a ceasefire agreement (typically dated to late 2022 or early 2024, depending on which ceasefire is referenced).
verified_facts.note: Confirmed by news reports; the exact dates and terms of ceasefire(s) vary by source and framing.

verified_facts.statement: The United States maintains military presence in Iraqi Kurdistan, including at bases such as Harir Airbase and Erbil Airport.
verified_facts.note: Publicly acknowledged by US government; scale and mission scope are sometimes disputed.

verified_facts.statement: Kurdish opposition groups operating from Iraqi Kurdistan have been reported to receive support from external actors, including the United States.
verified_facts.note: Reported by major news outlets; the extent, legality, and nature of support remain contested.

verified_facts.statement: The Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) has limited ability to prevent IRGC strikes within its territory.
verified_facts.source_url: https://www.aljazeera.com or statements by KRG officials
verified_facts.note: Acknowledged by KRG leadership and international observers; the reasons (military capability, political constraints, or both) are debated.

unverified_shared_claims.statement: Specific casualty counts (civilian vs. combatant) from individual strikes.
unverified_shared_claims.note: Different sources report conflicting numbers; no independent verification mechanism exists for all incidents. Framings cite different casualty figures to support their narratives.

unverified_shared_claims.statement: The precise number of post-ceasefire IRGC strikes and their timing relative to ceasefire terms.
unverified_shared_claims.note: Depends on which ceasefire agreement is referenced and how 'post-ceasefire' is defined. Sources disagree on whether strikes violated specific terms.

unverified_shared_claims.statement: Whether specific strikes intentionally targeted civilian infrastructure (schools, medical facilities) or struck them as collateral damage.
unverified_shared_claims.note: Requires evidence of intent; satellite imagery and eyewitness accounts are contested. No independent investigation with full access has been completed.

unverified_shared_claims.statement: The operational status, military capability, and cross-border attack frequency of Kurdish opposition groups.
unverified_shared_claims.note: Iranian sources emphasize imminent threat; Western and Kurdish sources dispute the scale and imminence. No agreed baseline exists.

unverified_shared_claims.statement: The extent and nature of CIA/Mossad support to Kurdish opposition groups.
unverified_shared_claims.note: Iranian and some regional sources assert direct arming and coordination; US and Israeli governments deny or minimize involvement. Declassified evidence is limited.

unverified_shared_claims.statement: Whether IRGC strikes constitute violations of international humanitarian law or are lawful acts of self-defense.
unverified_shared_claims.note: Legal determination depends on contested factual premises (intent, civilian presence, military necessity) and interpretation of IHL. No international court has ruled.

points_of_disagreement: Whether the Kurdish opposition groups pose a genuine, imminent military threat to Iran or are primarily political/symbolic targets.
Whether IRGC strikes are preemptive self-defense or disproportionate attacks on civilian populations and refugee camps.
The degree to which the US and Israel are arming, directing, or coordinating with Kurdish opposition groups vs. providing limited or no support.
Whether the strikes violate Iraqi sovereignty in a way that demands international intervention or are a legitimate response to cross-border threats.
Whether civilian casualties are incidental to military targeting or evidence of systematic targeting of non-combatants.
Whether the ceasefire(s) have been violated by Iran or remain in effect with mutual understanding.
Whether the US should increase military support/presence to deter IRGC strikes or reduce involvement to de-escalate regional tensions.
Whether Kurdish opposition groups are terrorist organizations (Iranian framing) or legitimate political/resistance movements (Kurdish/Western framing).
The historical responsibility of the US and regional powers for the vulnerability of Kurdish populations to Iranian strikes.
shared_foundation.summary: All framings accept that the IRGC conducted multiple missile and drone strikes on targets in Sulaymaniyah Governorate associated with Kurdish opposition groups, that civilian areas were present in or near strike zones, that the US maintains military presence in Iraqi Kurdistan, and that the KRG has limited ability to prevent such strikes. The fundamental disagreements concern the military threat posed by the opposition groups, the intent and proportionality of the strikes, the role of external powers (US, Israel) in arming or directing those groups, and whether the strikes constitute lawful self-defense or violations of international law and Iraqi sovereignty.

framings.name: Iranian Counter-Terrorism / Preemptive Defense
framings.question: Did Iran have a legitimate right to strike armed groups preparing to cross its border and destabilize its territory?
framings.key_claim: The IRGC strikes are a justified preemptive operation against armed separatist terrorist groups backed by the US and Israel who were preparing to invade Iranian soil from Iraqi Kurdistan.
framings.description: This framing, originating from Iranian state institutions, characterizes the Kurdish opposition groups as foreign-backed terrorist organizations using Iraqi territory as a rear base to threaten Iran's sovereignty and territorial integrity. The strikes are presented as a lawful act of national self-defense.
framings.emphasizes: The groups' alleged CIA/Mossad ties, their stated intent to cross into Iran, Iran's 'right of preemptive defense,' and the groups' own military activities and cross-border attacks against Iran.
framings.downplays: Civilian casualties, the refugee/asylum-seeker status of many camp residents, international humanitarian law, and Iraqi sovereignty violations.
sample_headlines: IRGC strikes terrorist groups headquarters in Iraqi Kurdistan region
Iran says it targeted 'terrorist groups' in Iraqi Kurdistan

carriers.name: IRNA (Islamic Republic News Agency)
carriers.excerpt: "The headquarters of terrorist groups in Sulaymaniyah, Iraq, was hit," the IRGC said in a brief statement, as reported by IRNA.
carriers.role_evidence: IRNA is the official Islamic Republic mouthpiece; its Telegram post was the first and primary vehicle for the Iranian government's framing of the strikes.

carriers.name: Press TV
carriers.excerpt: Iran has intensified its campaign against these groups following reports that the United States and Israel have been attempting to arm and mobilize Kurdish militias to fight against Iran.
carriers.role_evidence: Iran's English-language state broadcaster used the 'terrorist' label and amplified the CIA/Mossad narrative to an international audience.

carriers.name: Iran Intelligence Ministry
carriers.excerpt: "Separatist terrorist groups intended to enter the country through the western borders, with the support of the American and Zionist enemy."
carriers.role_evidence: The ministry issued formal statements endorsing the preemptive-defense framing, describing joint IRGC-intelligence operations.

carriers.name: Ali Larijani (Iran Supreme National Security Council Secretary)
carriers.excerpt: "Separatist groups should not think that a breeze has blown and try to take action. We will not tolerate them in any way."
carriers.role_evidence: Senior official statement formally backing the 'preemptive defense' justification.

carriers.name: Times of Israel / AFP (as news reporters)
carriers.excerpt: Iran's IRNA news agency posts on Telegram: "The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has targeted the headquarters of terrorist groups in Sulaymaniyah, Iraq."
carriers.role_evidence: Neutral relay of Iran's official framing without endorsing the 'terrorist' label.

framings.name: Human Cost / Civilian Harm
framings.question: Who are the actual victims on the ground, and what is the documented toll on civilians, refugees, and families?
framings.key_claim: IRGC strikes systematically target not just armed fighters but also civilian refugee camps, family residences, schools, and medical facilities, placing thousands of Kurdish civilians—including women and children—at grave risk in violation of international humanitarian law.
framings.description: This framing, advanced primarily by Kurdish human rights organizations and peace groups, centers the lived experience of refugees, asylum seekers, and civilian families caught in the strikes. It draws on granular incident documentation to argue the attacks constitute violations of the Geneva Conventions and IHL.
framings.emphasizes: Casualty counts, civilian infrastructure damage, refugee/UNHCR-protected status of camp residents, attacks continuing despite ceasefire, specific victims such as 18-year-old Ghazal Mawlan.
framings.downplays: The military activities of opposition groups, the broader US-Iran war context, and geopolitical justifications on any side.
sample_headlines: Decade of IRGC missile, drone attacks on Kurdish party bases, refugee camps in Iraqi Kurdistan (2017–2026)
IRGC missile and drone attacks target civilian camps and Kurdish opposition bases in Iraq's Kurdistan Region

carriers.name: Kurdistan Human Rights Network (KHRN)
carriers.excerpt: These camps serve not only as bases for party members but as homes for their families, many of whom hold refugee status under the Geneva Conventions.
carriers.role_evidence: Published the most comprehensive longitudinal documentation of the strikes and their civilian impact, spanning 2017–2026.

carriers.name: Hengaw Organization for Human Rights
carriers.excerpt: Civilian infrastructure, including residential buildings, schools, medical centers, and libraries, has also been hit.
carriers.role_evidence: Produced real-time statistical documentation of 112+ attacks and named civilian infrastructure targets, widely cited by international media.

carriers.name: Christian Peacemaker Teams – Iraqi Kurdistan (CPT-IK)
carriers.excerpt: Civilian areas, civilian institutions, and Peshmerga bases – none of which are parties to the conflict – were targeted 172 times (36.29%).
carriers.role_evidence: Field-verified attack documentation with disaggregated civilian vs. military targeting data, providing independent corroboration.

carriers.name: Wikipedia – 2026 Iranian Strikes on the Kurdistan Region (community-sourced)
carriers.excerpt: Ghazal Mawlan, an 18-year-old female member of the Komala of the Toilers of Kurdistan, succumbed to wounds sustained in an Iranian strike on 14 April.
carriers.role_evidence: Aggregated civilian harm documentation—including the Ghazal Mawlan hospital-denial incident—into a widely-referenced public article.

carriers.name: KRG Ministry of Peshmerga Affairs
carriers.excerpt: "Between 28 February and 20 April 2026, the Kurdistan Region was subjected to 809 attacks. These resulted in the deaths of 20 civilians and left 123 others injured."
carriers.role_evidence: Official KRG government figures lending institutional weight to the civilian-harm framing.

framings.name: Iraqi Sovereignty Violation
framings.question: Does Iran's cross-border military action inside Iraqi territory constitute an illegal violation of a sovereign state's territorial integrity?
framings.key_claim: Repeated IRGC missile and drone strikes inside Iraq's Kurdistan Region represent a flagrant and sustained violation of Iraqi sovereignty that Baghdad has been unable or unwilling to effectively counter.
framings.description: This framing treats the strikes first and foremost as a foreign-policy and international-law crisis for Iraq as a state, rather than as a Kurdish or Iranian-domestic issue. It examines whether Baghdad can or should assert control and what the strikes mean for Iraqi political stability, government formation, and regional standing.
framings.emphasizes: Iraq's treaty obligations, Baghdad's political paralysis, Iran's disregard for Iraqi borders, and the destabilizing effect on Iraq's sovereignty and Gulf relations.
framings.downplays: The military character of the Kurdish groups being struck, and the US/Israel role in the wider war.
sample_headlines: Iraq Unable to Avoid the U.S.-Iran Crossfire
Iran-Aligned Militias Jeopardize Iraq's Gulf Reset

carriers.name: Foreign Policy (Mina Al-Oraibi)
carriers.excerpt: These developments represent an Iranian-backed effort to undercut the largely stable Kurdistan Region and its KDP leadership.
carriers.role_evidence: Among the earliest long-form US analyses to center the Iraqi-sovereignty framing in the context of the broader strikes.

carriers.name: The Soufan Center
carriers.excerpt: Despite their best efforts, leaders in both the national government in Baghdad and the semi-autonomous Kurdish-controlled north have failed to keep the U.S.-Iran conflict out of Iraqi territory.
carriers.role_evidence: Issued an early intelligence brief foregrounding Iraq's sovereignty dilemma and its inability to remain neutral.

carriers.name: Stimson Center
carriers.excerpt: Baghdad's problem is no longer simply that Iraqi sovereignty is being violated by non-state actors.
carriers.role_evidence: Think-tank analysis explicitly framing the strikes as a structural challenge to Iraqi state authority.

carriers.name: Manara Magazine
carriers.excerpt: Each iteration erodes the authority of the state and reinforces the perception that Iraq is both a battlefield and a launch point.
carriers.role_evidence: Published a French-origin analysis translated to English that explicitly named Iraq's sovereignty erosion as the central story.

carriers.name: Iraqi Federal Government (PM al-Sudani / NSA al-Araji statements)
carriers.excerpt: Iraq will not allow groups 'to infiltrate or cross the Iranian border to carry out terrorist acts from Iraqi territory.'
carriers.role_evidence: Baghdad's official condemnation of strikes on its territory, adopting sovereignty framing even while being constrained by Iran-aligned internal forces.

framings.name: US-Israel Proxy War / Regime Change by Other Means
framings.question: Are these strikes Iran's defensive response to a US-Israeli project using Kurdish groups as proxy instruments to foment regime change in Tehran?
framings.key_claim: The IRGC strikes are a direct response to a CIA and US-Israeli program to arm, fund, and deploy Kurdish opposition groups as proxy forces to destabilize western Iran and open a 'second front' against the Islamic Republic.
framings.description: This framing contextualizes the strikes within the 2026 US-Iran war, arguing that the Kurdish groups are not simply organic opposition but have been activated as instruments of US/Israeli strategic policy—making the strikes a defensive military response to a foreign-backed covert operation rather than an unprovoked aggression.
framings.emphasizes: Reported CIA arming program, Trump's personal calls to Kurdish leaders, Israeli ground-preparation strikes on the Iraq-Iran border, and the groups' own stated intent to topple the Iranian regime.
framings.downplays: The long pre-existing history of IRGC attacks on these groups well before CIA involvement, civilian casualties in the strikes, and the agency and political rights of Kurdish communities.
sample_headlines: CIA working to arm Kurdish forces to spark uprising in Iran, sources say
IRGC Strikes on Iraq's Kurdistan Region Prevent Kurdish Offensive in 2026 Conflict

carriers.name: CNN Politics (national security correspondents)
carriers.excerpt: The CIA is working to arm Kurdish forces with the aim of fomenting a popular uprising in Iran, multiple people familiar with the plan told CNN.
carriers.role_evidence: First major US outlet to break the CIA-arming story, which anchored the proxy-war framing in mainstream American discourse.

carriers.name: Press TV / IRNA (Iran state media)
carriers.excerpt: Iran has intensified its campaign against these groups following reports that the United States and Israel have been attempting to arm and mobilize Kurdish militias.
carriers.role_evidence: Iranian state media adopted and amplified the proxy framing globally to justify the strikes as counterterrorism against Western proxies.

carriers.name: The Defense News (analysis piece)
carriers.excerpt: Iran's IRGC prevented Iranian Kurdish opposition groups from opening a western front during the ongoing conflict involving Iran, the United States, and Israel.
carriers.role_evidence: Provided detailed military analysis framing the strikes as a successful Iranian counter-proxy operation.

carriers.name: Times of Israel / AP (wire relay)
carriers.excerpt: Trump had personally spoken to Kurdish leaders in recent days and requested their assistance in the campaign.
carriers.role_evidence: Relayed AP/WashPost reporting on Trump's direct calls to Kurdish leaders, cementing the US-proxy dimension in broad US readership.

carriers.name: White House / Pete Hegseth (pushback)
carriers.excerpt: "None of our objectives are premised on the support or the arming of any particular force," Hegseth said.
carriers.role_evidence: Trump administration officially denied the arming narrative, acting as a partial critic of the proxy-war framing even as reports persisted.

framings.name: Ceasefire Violation / Diplomatic Impunity
framings.question: Does Iran's continuation of strikes on Kurdish groups after the April 2026 ceasefire expose a pattern of bad faith and impunity that undermines peace negotiations?
framings.key_claim: Iran's post-ceasefire IRGC strikes on Kurdish camps demonstrate that Tehran treats the ceasefire as selectively applicable, continuing attacks against Kurds with near-total international impunity while nominally complying with the US-Iran truce.
framings.description: This framing, prominent in defense-policy and Kurdish diaspora outlets, argues that the IRGC's continuation of drone and missile strikes even after the April 8 ceasefire is a deliberate demonstration of impunity—revealing a double standard in which attacks on Kurds are ignored while the US-Iran dimension of the conflict receives diplomatic attention.
framings.emphasizes: Continued strikes after ceasefire, number of post-ceasefire attacks, lack of international response, and the contrast between US-Iran negotiations and ongoing Kurdish targeting.
framings.downplays: The internal logic of Iranian security concerns and the legal ambiguities over whether Kurdish groups fall under the ceasefire scope.
sample_headlines: Iran relentlessly targets Kurdish opposition in northern Iraq despite regional ceasefire
Despite ceasefire, IRGC launches 18 attacks on Kurdistan parties' camps, leaving 4 dead and 9 injured

carriers.name: Hengaw Organization for Human Rights
carriers.excerpt: Despite ceasefire, IRGC launches 18 attacks on Kurdistan parties' camps, leaving 4 dead and 9 injured.
carriers.role_evidence: First to systematically document and headline the ceasefire-violation dimension of continued IRGC strikes on Kurdish camps.

carriers.name: The Jerusalem Post / Seth J. Frantzman (FDD)
carriers.excerpt: Although there is a ceasefire between Iran and the US, Iran has continued the attacks against the Kurdistan Region.
carriers.role_evidence: FDD-affiliated analyst repeatedly highlighted the ceasefire-violation framing in widely-read analysis pieces.

carriers.name: FDD's Long War Journal
carriers.excerpt: The attacks on the Kurdistan Region are part of Iran's continued attacks in the region, despite the ceasefire with the US.
carriers.role_evidence: Defense-policy outlet with large security-community readership consistently framed post-ceasefire Kurdish strikes as Iranian bad faith.

carriers.name: JINSA (Jewish Institute for National Security of America)
carriers.excerpt: Iran's sustained targeting of the KRG itself, even after the Pakistan-brokered ceasefire, reflects a deeper agenda.
carriers.role_evidence: Policy brief explicitly arguing that post-ceasefire strikes reveal a strategic Iranian agenda beyond legitimate counter-terrorism.

carriers.name: Trita Parsi / Quincy Institute (critic of the framing)
carriers.excerpt: Trump had become increasingly desperate for a deal with Iran to the point of even denying ceasefire violations by Iran to maintain it.
carriers.role_evidence: Argued the ceasefire-violation framing was being selectively deployed by the Trump administration and hawks to sabotage diplomacy.

framings.name: Kurdish Self-Determination vs. Regional Abandonment
framings.question: Are the Kurdish groups—long-standing aspirants to political rights and autonomy—being used as pawns by great powers who will ultimately abandon them?
framings.key_claim: Kurdish opposition groups operating from Iraqi Kurdistan face existential IRGC strikes with inadequate protection from the US or KRG, repeating a painful historical pattern in which Kurds are instrumentalized in great-power conflicts and then left to absorb the consequences.
framings.description: This framing, prominent in Kurdish diaspora media and some left-leaning Western commentary, centers Kurdish political agency and the history of betrayal. It acknowledges the military activities of the groups but argues their vulnerability reflects a structural abandonment—especially as the US engages in ceasefire diplomacy without conditions protecting Kurdish groups.
framings.emphasizes: Decades of prior IRGC strikes, the groups' refugee and exile origins post-1979, KRG leaders' fear and inability to refuse US pressure, and the historical pattern of US abandonment of Kurdish allies.
framings.downplays: The active military role of the groups, the operational details of CIA support, and the IRGC's security justifications.
sample_headlines: Iranian Kurd leader in Iraq says ground operation into Iran 'highly likely'
Kurdish News Briefing: IRGC Drone Strikes, U.S. Exits Rojava & Kurdish President Elected in Iraq

carriers.name: Kurdish History / Kurdish diaspora media network
carriers.excerpt: For the Kurdish people, this week has brought both loss and consequence.
carriers.role_evidence: Explicitly frames Kurdish suffering through the lens of abandonment—IRGC strikes alongside US withdrawal from Rojava as parallel betrayals.

carriers.name: Al Jazeera
carriers.excerpt: "We have been planning for a long time, and now that conditions are more favourable, there is a strong probability of action."
carriers.role_evidence: Gave Kurdish leaders direct voice to articulate their own framing of the stakes, situating them as actors rather than merely victims or proxies.

carriers.name: Iran International
carriers.excerpt: Several Iranian Kurdish opposition parties...have generally framed their demands around political rights and Kurdish self-rule within Iran.
carriers.role_evidence: Largest Persian-language opposition broadcaster; consistently frames Kurdish groups as political actors with legitimate autonomy/federalism goals.

carriers.name: CNN (background reporting)
carriers.excerpt: Many Trump administration officials have privately warned of the disillusionment Kurdish forces have felt when working with the US in the past.
carriers.role_evidence: Noted the abandonment dynamic in sourced reporting but did not center it as the primary frame.

carriers.name: Senior KRG Official (quoted)
carriers.excerpt: "We are very frightened."
carriers.role_evidence: KRG officials' own expressions of fear and powerlessness align with the abandonment framing in their public and background statements.

framings.name: US Strategic Partnership / Threat to American Interests
framings.question: Do the IRGC strikes threaten the Kurdistan Region as a critical US strategic partner and military hub, requiring Washington to respond more forcefully?
framings.key_claim: Iran's strikes on Iraqi Kurdistan directly threaten US military assets, energy investments, and a vital anti-Iran partner in the region, demanding a stronger American response to protect a key strategic alliance.
framings.description: This framing, dominant in US hawkish policy institutions and defense media, treats the strikes primarily through the lens of American strategic interest—the KRG as a hosting base for US troops, a hub for US energy companies, and the last part of Iraq where Iran has not established dominant influence. It calls for policy action.
framings.emphasizes: US basing rights (Harir Airbase, Erbil Airport), Chevron/ExxonMobil investments, the KRG's counterterrorism partnership, and Iran's agenda of driving a US-KRG wedge.
framings.downplays: The Kurdish groups' own armed activities and the broader US-Iran war dynamics that provoked the escalation.
sample_headlines: Iranian Attacks on Iraqi Kurdistan Threaten a Vital U.S. Partnership
U.S. facilities in Iraq have experienced over 600 attacks since the onset of war

carriers.name: JINSA (Jewish Institute for National Security of America)
carriers.excerpt: The KRG is also the only part of Iraq where Iran and its aligned militias have been unable to penetrate and exert significant political and economic influence.
carriers.role_evidence: JINSA was among the first to publish a formal policy brief centering the US-strategic-interest framing with specific recommendations to Washington.

carriers.name: FDD / Long War Journal (Seth J. Frantzman)
carriers.excerpt: The US has increased efforts to target Iranian-backed militias in Iraq.
carriers.role_evidence: FDD's reporting and analysis consistently embeds Kurdish strikes in the US strategic competition with Iran, reaching a large policy-community audience.

carriers.name: The Wall Street Journal
carriers.excerpt: "U.S. facilities in Iraq have experienced over 600 attacks since the onset of war," underscoring how Iran-aligned militias have turned the country into a major proxy battleground.
carriers.role_evidence: WSJ's aggregated attack figures helped mass audiences understand Iraqi Kurdistan as a front-line American security concern.

carriers.name: US State Department / Rewards for Justice Program
carriers.excerpt: The US State Department's Rewards for Justice Program offered a $10 million reward for information on Harakat Hezbollah al Nujaba leader Akram Abbas al Kabi.
carriers.role_evidence: Four successive US rewards for Iranian-militia leaders in Iraq signal official US adoption of the 'threat to American interests' framing.

framings.name: International Law / IHL Accountability
framings.question: Do the strikes violate international humanitarian law, including protections for refugees, civilians, and political asylum seekers?
framings.key_claim: The IRGC's repeated drone and missile attacks on UNHCR-recognized refugee camps, family residences, schools, and medical facilities constitute violations of international humanitarian law and protections owed to political asylum seekers under the Geneva Conventions.
framings.description: This framing, advanced by human rights legal bodies and diaspora-linked advocacy networks, scrutinizes the strikes specifically through the standards of IHL—the laws of armed conflict, distinction between combatants and civilians, and the protected status of refugee populations. It calls for UN and international legal intervention.
framings.emphasizes: Refugee and UNHCR status of camp residents, destruction of humanitarian infrastructure, the distinction principle under IHL, and the targeting of areas explicitly outside active hostilities.
framings.downplays: Operational security justifications for the strikes, the armed character of some group members, and bilateral US-Iran war dynamics.
sample_headlines: Kurdistan Human Rights Network condemns IRGC missile and drone attacks, calls on international community to act
Hengaw states that continuation of attacks constitutes a clear violation of international humanitarian law

carriers.name: Kurdistan Human Rights Network (KHRN)
carriers.excerpt: These camps serve not only as bases for party members but as homes for their families, many of whom hold refugee status under the Geneva Conventions.
carriers.role_evidence: First to frame the strikes systematically as violations of specific IHL instruments, including the Geneva Conventions and UNHCR mandate.

carriers.name: Hengaw Organization for Human Rights
carriers.excerpt: The Hengaw Organization for Human Rights calls on the international community, the UN Special Rapporteur on Iran, and global human rights bodies to take immediate action.
carriers.role_evidence: Explicitly invoked the UN Special Rapporteur mechanism, framing the attacks as IHL violations requiring international legal response.

carriers.name: CPT Iraqi Kurdistan
carriers.excerpt: The Iraqi government must also take responsibility by pursuing diplomatic efforts to protect the Kurdistan Region and to hold accountable all groups and actors.
carriers.role_evidence: Field documentation explicitly names state accountability as an IHL obligation, calling on both Iraqi and international bodies.

carriers.name: ACLED (Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project)
carriers.excerpt: Between February 28 and March 31, 2026, Iran and allied forces launched at least 388 missiles and drones into Iraq's Kurdistan Region.
carriers.role_evidence: ACLED's neutral conflict data is used by IHL advocates to substantiate the scale of attacks for legal accountability arguments.

gap_analysis: Missing: the IRGC's stated operational/tactical rationale beyond counter-terrorism framing (e.g., specific intelligence claims, threat assessment methodology). Missing: the Kurdish opposition group's own perspective—their political platform, why they're designated as threats by Iran vs. viewed as legitimate resistance by others, and their civilian support base. Missing: Iraq's internal political fractures—Sunni/Shia/Kurdish government dynamics and whether Baghdad tacitly permits or opposes these strikes. Missing: Turkey's role and interests (PKK connections, regional balance-of-power concerns). Missing: humanitarian/refugee flow impacts and local economic disruption beyond casualty counts.
